So, as much as you can, try to incorporate both of those elements in your story. That is the definition of a good climax. And the fifth question you should ask is, are the stakes super high? The definition of a climactic moment is when the stakes are the very highest. You know, death is on the line. Love is on the line. Their very identity or soul is on the line. If you're not making the reader worried like, oh no, the absolute worst thing possible might just happen, then you don't really have a climax. And woof, there it is. You are done. She's been missing for 2 weeks, and he asks whether the mother is with the person that he's calling. Nope. And then the mystery intensifies because the woman that he called says, "You know what? You shouldn't look for her." Oh, huh. And then she tells him, "Never call me again." Now, this is very much a literary novel, but from an opening like that, you would almost think this was like a hard-boiled detective novel or like a thriller or something. I won't spoil the book by revealing what happens, but I will say the strategy of starting with some sort of mystery on the very first page of your book is a great way to start a book. And now it's time for number eight. And number eight is ground the public in the personal. So, at the beginning of Tom Perrotta's The Leftovers, we have this worldwide mass disappearance of 140 million people. They just vanish up in the thin air. Nobodies. But, that first chapter story is told through a single one who was left behind, Laura Garvey. And so, this broad event is filtered through her consciousness. Her talking to her kid about religion and why this event wasn't the rapture. How she deals with a world in which people just up and vanish. And then also how she ends up comforting people who had loved ones suddenly disappear on them. Sidebar, it's really a book in a series about how to deal with grief. But my larger point is the way into a big story is always through a small portal, a single person's experience of that event. So don't feel like you have to tackle the enormity of a worldwide event, just tell what one person did. And our last point is number nine, offer someone to root for. In Slumdog Millionaire by Vikas Swarup, we get to know the main character, Ram Mohammed Thomas. And by the way, in the movie his name was changed to Jamal Malik. But I like the first name because it shows that he's an everyman, right? The The first name is Hindu, the second name is Muslim, the third name is Christian. But what I think the author does really well is he gives us lots of reasons from the very beginning to be cheering for this character. One, we know that he's smart, right? He just won a game show. So we're like, "Oh, good job, buddy. Like, amazing." Two, we know that he's very poor and that the rich people resent him for being poor and still being able to answer all these questions. Three, we see that he gets arrested for zero reason whatsoever and that makes us sympathetic towards him. Lastly, he is tortured and they try to make him confess to cheating on the show even though he did not cheat at all. So we like Ram right away. We are on his side, we are invested in the story and we want to see him succeed. If you like this video and you want more information about first chapters, my book The Lynchpin Writer has a whole chapter specifically on how to start the first chapter of your book. So I'd recommend getting that and checking it out.

it can even make your dialogue mean the exact opposite of what is plainly there on the page I think the danger here is that if she says like oh I love you like it comes off as being a little bit too cheesy so the author is guarding against that by having her say the opposite of what she really intends so here's a little exercise go through your story and look at any point where a character is saying directly what they mean now some of the time you want to keep it right in certain pivotal scenes like you want them to be direct but for other scenes try having them talk around it or try having them hint at it but not directly say it and see if the other character can understand what they mean and if you want more instruction on how to write dialogue check out my course The Ultimate Guide to writing dialogue the link is in the description

constantly modulating what we're thinking in our heads and what actually comes out of our mouth your character should be doing that too even what your character will say to one person they wouldn't dare say it to someone else so remember dialogue is not the place where you just get an unfiltered stream of what enters into your character's mind but dialogue is really the physical embodiment of Where all the characters basically sound the same. Really, they sound like you. You should try to graduate to the second level. Which is where characters sound different, but they're still saying exactly what you want them to say. Basically, they're all your mouthpiece. For instance, the characters that you hate are sort of giving a straw man version of themselves and their ideas. Level three is true polyphony. This is where all your characters think and speak in a way that's completely unique to them. Doesn't feel like you're a ventriloquist. It feels like they're really real people.

Primary Topic: Character

Tertiary Topics: Writing Craft
Source Lines: 3070-3081

### Transcript

Kind: captions Language: en Here are three ways to make your characters more likable. But, just a reminder that characters don't have to be likable. They really only have to be compelling. Likable also doesn't mean flawless. Mary Sue characters are likable, but fake. One, a strong morality. In Cormac McCarthy's All the Pretty Horses, John Grady Cole has a really strong inner conviction about what's right and wrong. Makes him really likable as a character. Two, have your characters do a small act of charity or show kindness to a child. In A Man Called Ove, Ove takes care of a stray cat, and even though he's super curmudgeonly, we like him because he's caring for the cat. Three, make your characters suffer. Offred from The Handmaid's Tale suffers so much, and we like her because we feel sympathy for her.

### Transcript

Kind: captions Language: en Here are three tips to help you out when you're writing dialogue. If these three tips are helpful, get my book The Lynchpin Writer or take my dialogue writing course. If you do these three tips already, kudos to you. Usually, I find that most writers forget about one or two of them. One, use misunderstandings. I don't just mean mishearing someone, although that is a good technique. I mean two characters really talking past each other. Two, don't always have your character say exactly what they think. I'm not talking about lying, although it's good to have your characters lie. I'm talking about characters hedging and hinting at things rather than saying it outright. Three, give every character their own unique verbal tic. Your goal is to make them sound different than your other characters. Give a character an interjection, have them use a lot of slang, or have them be super formal, or have them talk in brief or long sentences.

So, Scott Snyder sent one of his short stories into a literary journal. They sent back a form rejection. He's like, "All right, that's fine. I'll just send it out again." Well, a month later they sent him another rejection. He's like, "Did you really have to reject it twice? I mean, I got the message the first time." But, that wasn't the end of it. A month later from then they sent out a third rejection letter to him. And he's like, "Dude, I got it. You don't want the story. That's okay." But, that's not the end of the story. About 6 months after that, he was doing a reading and he read that particular short story. And the editor of the literary journal that had rejected him three times came up to him afterwards and was like, "Hey, I really love that short story. Would you be willing to publish it in my literary journal?" And he didn't mention that you've already rejected me three times for this. He said, "Well, yes. Sure. Sure, I will." And he ended up publishing in that same literary journal. Perseverance is the key for every single writer.

## When To Write A Prologue

Transcript ID: `TX-E1G9OgIb5B8`  
Video ID: E1G9OgIb5B8  
Title: When To Write A Prologue  
Date: 20221102  
Source URL: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E1G9OgIb5B8  
Transcript source: Automatic captions  
Caption language: en  
Primary Topic: Scene Craft
Secondary Topics: Character, Genre
Tertiary Topics: Prologues, Genre, Omniscient Narration, First Chapter, Limited Third, Reader Engagement
Source Lines: 3994-4005

### Transcript

Kind: captions Language: en 95% of the time you should not be writing a prologue, but if you choose to write a prologue, here's how you do it. One, I feel like prologues tend to work better with omniscient points of view. It's not to say that you can't do it if you have a limited third or first person or something like that, but in general, I would say most of the time it works better with omniscient. Two, prologues often work better if you're starting that prologue with characters who aren't the main characters. If that's the right place to begin the book, then that would be the time to make it a prologue, and so the reader knows like, "Oh, the first chapter is going to be the real characters. This prologue is sort of like backstory setup." Number three, if the beginning of your novel takes place in a time period that's far different than where your main story takes place, that's a good place for a prologue, too. And number four, if you are writing a genre that is friendly to prologues, some genres are just not friendly to prologues, and they're sort of looked down upon. So, look, if you're writing something like fantasy or sci-fi or something like that, they often have prologues, and they work quite fine. So, it depends on your genre.
